query: Which continuous noising formulation explains why low-NFE adaptive probability-flow sampling can still preserve sample quality under a continuum of diffusion distributions?
answer: The middle samples remain realistic even at NFE=14, while the left plot shows looser precision uses far fewer evaluations, so adaptive probability-flow sampling can be efficient without obvious quality loss. The bridge explains this by replacing finitely many noise distributions with "a continuum of distributions that evolve over time according to a diffusion process" and a prescribed SDE that progressively diffuses data into noise. That continuum is instantiated by the sub-VP SDE, \(\mathrm d \mathbf x = - \tfrac { 1 } { 2 } \beta ( t ) \mathbf x \, \mathrm d t + \sqrt { \beta ( t ) } \, \mathrm d \mathbf w\), which provides the continuous noising formulation.

The bridge states that "the neural network is responsible for prediction of the distribution p_ ( _0| _t)" and that "the input to the neural network covers all modalities," which motivates going beyond simple self-attention. The bridge explicitly links this to deployability by stating, "No need for dozens of devices, one or two are enough to run 70B models" and "Without the memory scheduler, full weights are loaded onto the devices," explaining why scheduling makes smaller-device setups possible. Given that feasibility, the latency outcome is that the Llama 2-70B device-scaling bars drop from about 51 s/token at 4 devices to about 26 s/token at 8 devices. So memory scheduling enables 70B operation on few devices, while adding more devices improves latency substantially.
